subject: zoology
question_text: What are lateral appendages? Based on their presence and absence, write the various types of flagella giving at least one example for each type.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section, SAQ chapter 8 'Locomotion & Reproduction' (book p.41, question 39). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this card, not merely unrun; 'not checked' must never be read as 'checked and clean'. The mark split is this card's claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. APPEARANCES: the book prints [AP,TS M-15,17]. ORDER CHANGED, CONTENT KEPT: the book lists the five types in the order stichonematic, pantonematic, acronematic, pantacronematic, anematic. This card regroups the same five as three WITH mastigonemes and two WITHOUT, because the question itself asks for the types 'based on their presence and absence'. No type, definition or example is changed. BOOK SPELLING: the book prints 'Chilomonas and cryptomonas' and 'Peranema, Monas' in lower case in places; the genus names are capitalised here. FIGURE SCOPE: the book prints the five types lettered A to E with the axoneme marked; this figure draws the same five and labels each with its type name.

steps.label: Lateral appendages
lines: Some flagella carry one, two or many rows of
short hair-like fibrils along their sides.
These fibrils are called lateral appendages,
or mastigonemes.
The central shaft of the flagellum is the
axoneme. The mastigonemes stand out from it.
Flagella are classified into five types by the
presence or absence of these mastigonemes.
steps.why: Every one of the five type names is built from the mastigoneme arrangement, so the classification cannot be written until the word mastigoneme has been defined.
common_mistakes: Calling the mastigonemes cilia. They are fine fibrils on the side of one flagellum, not separate organelles.
Leaving out the second name. Lateral appendages and mastigonemes are the same thing, and either may be asked for.
steps.memory_tip: Mastigoneme means a thread on a whip: the side hairs on the flagellum shaft.
steps.margin_note: Define the word first, then say five types follow from it.

steps.label: Types with mastigonemes
lines: 1. Stichonematic: the flagellum bears ONE row
of mastigonemes. Example: Euglena, Astasia.
2. Pantonematic: the flagellum bears TWO or
more rows. Example: Peranema, Monas.
3. Pantacronematic: two or more rows of
mastigonemes and a naked terminal filament at
the tip. Example: Urceolus.
steps.why: These three differ only in how many rows of mastigonemes there are, so writing the number of rows against each name is what separates them on the answer sheet.
common_mistakes: Swapping sticho- and panto-. Sticho- is one row; panto- is two or more.
Giving no example. The question asks for at least one for each type.
steps.memory_tip: Sticho- is one row, panto- is many rows, and panta-acro- is many rows plus a bare tip.
steps.margin_note: Number of rows, then example, for each of the three. One line each.

steps.label: Types without mastigonemes
lines: 4. Acronematic: there are no mastigonemes.
The tip of the axoneme is naked, with no
sheath over it. Example: Chlamydomonas,
Polytoma.
5. Anematic, or simple: there are no
mastigonemes and no terminal filament.
Example: Chilomonas, Cryptomonas.
steps.why: Both of these types lack mastigonemes, so the only thing left to tell them apart is the terminal filament: the acronematic flagellum has a bare one, the anematic flagellum has none at all.
common_mistakes: Writing that an acronematic flagellum has mastigonemes. It has none; only its bare tip is named.
Treating anematic and acronematic as the same type. The terminal filament separates them.
steps.memory_tip: Acro- means tip, so acronematic is named for its bare tip; a- means none, so anematic has neither hairs nor tip filament.
steps.margin_note: Say what is ABSENT in each. That is what the question asks for.

steps.label: Diagram

elements.caption: Step 1 — five bare shafts on their cell bases
Step 2 — A stichonematic: one row of mastigonemes
Step 3 — B pantonematic: two rows of mastigonemes
Step 4 — C acronematic: a naked terminal filament
Step 5 — D pantacronematic: two rows and a naked tip
Step 6 — type names and labels; E stays plain

steps.why: The five types differ only in the mastigoneme rows and the tip, so five shafts drawn side by side make the whole classification readable in one look.
common_mistakes: Drawing all five the same and relying on the labels. The rows of mastigonemes must be visibly different.
Forgetting the bare terminal filament on types C and D.
steps.memory_tip: Draw the same bare shaft five times, then add: one row, two rows, two rows with a bare tip, a bare tip only, nothing.
steps.margin_note: Label each shaft A to E with its type name. The drawing carries the whole fourth mark.

insider_note: The examiner counts five type names and five examples — a student who writes perfect definitions but no examples usually loses half the marks on this question.
